title: A Unified Discrete and Continuous Theory of Core-Halo Complexity Maximizers
abstract: The maximization of statistical complexity has long been associated with the emergence of probability distributions lying between perfect order and complete disorder. While previous studies have shown that complexity-maximizing distributions exhibit a two-level structure in finite discrete systems, an analogous unified treatment for both discrete and continuous probability spaces has remained unavailable. In this work, we develop a general variational framework for a generalized statistical complexity constructed from Shannon and Renyi entropies. We derive a common stationary equation governing both discrete probability masses and continuous probability densities and prove that every stationary solution necessarily possesses exactly two probability levels, establishing a universal core-halo structure. We further demonstrate that the optimization problem reduces to a single multiplicity parameter and prove that the global complexity maximum is attained by the smallest admissible core, corresponding to a single dominant state in the discrete case and an infinitesimal core in the continuous limit. These results provide a complete analytical characterization of the complexity-maximizing distributions and reveal a common mathematical structure underlying complexity optimization in both discrete and continuous settings. The framework establishes a unified foundation for generalized statistical complexity with potential applications in statistical mechanics, information theory, and the analysis of complex systems.
summary: This paper unifies the characterization of statistical complexity across both discrete and continuous probability spaces using a generalized variational framework involving Shannon and Rényi entropies. It proves that any state maximizing this complexity must exhibit a universal two-level 'core-halo' structure. This provides a complete analytical tool for understanding how complex organization emerges mathematically in diverse physical systems.
main_problem: To develop a unified mathematical framework for quantifying statistical complexity that measures deviation from both perfect order and complete disorder.
main_result: The global maximum of the generalized statistical complexity is universally attained by distributions possessing exactly two probability levels (a core-halo structure), regardless of whether the underlying space is discrete or continuous.
method: The authors developed a general variational framework using Shannon and Rényi entropies, deriving common stationary equations applicable across both discrete and continuous probability spaces.
model_or_system: The theory applies to general probability distributions in both finite discrete systems (probability masses) and continuous probability spaces (densities). The complexity measure is generalized from standard entropy concepts.
key_observables: Generalized statistical complexity ($C_q$), Shannon Entropy ($H_1$), Rényi Entropies ($H_q$, $H_{2q}$), and the core-halo structure.
important_parameters: The multiplicity parameter ($m$) in discrete systems, and the continuous core measure ($M$); the optimization depends on these parameters.
main_assumptions: The framework assumes that complexity can be constructed from entropic measures and relies heavily on variational calculus techniques like the Envelope Theorem for simplification.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by first establishing the need for a unified measure, developing the generalized variational functional ($\Phi$), deriving common stationary equations for discrete/continuous cases, and finally using differentiation (Envelope Theorem) to prove that optimization leads to the smallest possible core size.
why_interesting: While not directly about quantum dynamics, the rigorous mathematical framework for characterizing emergent structure (core-halo) based on information theory is highly relevant for analyzing complexity in many-body quantum systems or open quantum systems far from equilibrium.
